newsitem.title: JORDAN: Middle East tension hurts Arab-Israel business.
newsitem.headline: Middle East tension hurts Arab-Israel business.

text.p: Arab and Israeli businessmen on Monday said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's tough policies had swept away hopes of growing Arab-Israeli business ties after landmark peace accords.

Since Netanyahu won elections last year on a pledge of a tougher policy towards Arabs, many businessmen see a hostile business climate undermining opportunities which arose after the 1993 Middle East peace accords.

"The environment which is prevalent right now is not one which is conducive to making business with Israel...and a lot of people are reluctant to do business with Israel these days," said Omar Salah, a leading Jordanian entrepreneur.

Israeli businessman Aric Brochstein, of Carmel Chemicals Ltd, said his firm had exported products to the Arab world but added: "Some people will tell you right in the first few sentences that they do not want to deal with you...They are ready to listen but do not want to deal."
Jordanian entrepreneur Salah runs Century Investment Group, a diversified industrial group.

Speaking on the sidelines of a European Union-sponsored fair at which 50 Israeli firms rubbed shoulders with Arab businessmen, he said business with Israeli firms was conducted in a less friendly environment and few new ventures were being struck.

"Since the Netanyahu era, the momentum has been lost. The business that was concluded at the time of the peace process probably still exists but goes on under a completely different environment," Salah said.

Zaki Ayoubi, an industrialist and board member of the Amman Chamber of Commerce, believes there are few prospects of growing business links as long as tension remains high among Arabs and Jews in Palestinian areas.

"Trade prospers in the presence of peaceful conditions and as long as there is tension in the Palestinian street, it will not be possible for trade exchanges to reach their desired dimension," Ayoubi said.

Salem Mashour, chairman of Cairo-based ECTRA, an agent for international machinery firms, said Israeli firms had approached him to do business but refused to do any deals "until the political climate improved".
But not everyone has slammed the door completely on dealings with Israel.
Businessmen say some Jordanian firms which lost traditional Gulf Arab markets after the Gulf crisis in 1990 were trying to offset losses by dealing with Israeli firms, especially in textiles.
Moroccan businesman Said el-Aarbaoui, who runs Casablanca-based textile firm Setafil, said he believed there was no difference between Israeli firms and others.
But Israeli businessmen, who put a brave face on a lack of widespread acceptance, also say the faltering fortunes of the peace process have taken their toll on the modest volume of trade so far.
Total trade with Jordan in the whole of 1996 did not exceed $14 million, while Israel's trade with Egypt, the first Arab state to make peace with 1979, was just $60 million.

"Those are the realities and it's very natural that there are suspicions, especially when the peace process is going down. At the same time they want to see what is going to happen in the near future," Mandy Barak, director of the Federation of Israeli Chamber of Commerce, told Reuters.

"I am a realist and I am sure it will take more than 25 years to have open trade between Israel and the region. Some countries will dismantle the barriers faster and some will do it much slower," Barak said.
